newsitem.title: USA: Strength in U.S. crudes grows on Brent tightness.
newsitem.headline: Strength in U.S. crudes grows on Brent tightness.

text.p: U.S. domestic crude markets were bouyed Monday afternoon on bullish North Sea Brent fundamentals and concerns over a fishermen's protest at Britain's main export terminal Sullom Voe, traders said.
June West Texas Intermediate/Cushing stood 85 cents higher at $21.25-35 a barrel, and maintained a 10-12 cents advantage over second month July WTI/Cushing.
North Sea fishermen amassed a flotilla of eleven small vessels to protest a delay in compensation payments resulting from the 1993 Braer tanker spill.
The test of whether the group can successfully stop loading operations for world benchmark Brent crude will likely come Tuesday, when a tanker is scheduled for arrival.
Traders said fallout from the protest aided prices for U.S. grades, notably Brent crude's key sweet competitor Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James.
LLS/St. James began trading this morning at nine cents over June WTI/Cushing, quickly accelerating to a 12 cents premium before slipping back to more modest levels.

Even without the flurry of Sullom Voe activity, LLS found underlying support late last week from more expensive cash Brent values, leaving domestic markets interested in local product instead of foreign barrels.

"The fishermen added to the fact that North Sea crude had firmed, lifting CFD's. There is not a lot of crude (North Sea) left, only two or three cargoes for June. It's a lot easier to pay for LLS at plus 10 cents (to benchmark WTI) than at Brent prices," said a cash trader in Texas.
Other domestic grades firmed, led by West Texas Sour/Midland trading hands at a $1.44 discount to benchmark.
"You'll hear the market talked at $1.50-43, but there is nobody going to sell it better than $1.43. It looks like you continue to have to pay-up a little for crude," a dealer said.
Traders said crude outrights tracked surging NYMEX prices.

NYMEX futures advanced on technical buying and concerns Middle East tensions may be stoked after Iran began a new set of wargames Sunday in the vital Strait of Hormuz, where much of the world's oil passes for export.

Iran has employed some 4,000 men, and various military components for the six-day exercise to enhance readiness. U.S. military leaders in the region vowed to keep sea lanes open, and stand firm against any threat.
